description: Lunar Shift is building Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a 3D Moon-base game for ages 7–12. Players repair solar panels, take shelter from a solar storm, and decide how to split limited battery power between life support and growing food. We already have a playable prototype in Rosebud and would love teammates interested in 3D art, game design, coding, or space science to help make the mission intuitive, fun, and grounded in real science.
summary:
Lunar Shift developed Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a playable 3D browser game that puts kids ages 7–12 in charge of a Moon base. Players explore in low gravity, repair two solar panels, and head to a shielded shelter when a solar storm warning arrives. On the way back, they see a ridge cast its shadow across the panels, forcing the base to switch to battery power.

Inside the shelter, there isn’t enough power to run both life support and the greenhouse through the shift. Players can keep backup air in reserve and delay the next harvest, or keep the grow lights on and use up the backup air. They can replay the decision and see what changes.

The storm scenario was inspired by an archived NASA solar-particle detection. The battery units and mission timing are simplified for play. By seeing what each choice protects and what it costs, young players learn why planning for the next emergency matters just as much as solving the one in front of them.
details:
Lunar Shift built Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, a playable 3D browser game for kids ages 7–12. Its first mission, Storm Shift, asks a simple question: when a Moon base can’t power everything, what do you protect now, and what do you save for later?

Players explore the base in low gravity and complete a separate repair minigame for each of two offline solar panels. A solar storm warning sends them to a shielded shelter. On the way back, they can see a ridge cast its shadow across the solar array, forcing the base to switch to stored power. We made these two events visibly different so players can connect each one to its consequence. The storm is why the crew goes inside. The shadow is why the base needs batteries.

At the shelter console, players choose between keeping backup air in reserve and keeping the next greenhouse harvest on schedule. Both plans protect the crew through the shift, but each comes at a cost. Players see what their choice changed and can try the other plan without replaying the repairs. The goal is for a child to explain the trade-off in their own words, not just reach a victory screen.

We built the prototype in Rosebud AI and designed it to run in a browser without special hardware. We used short instructions, one active objective at a time, and visible changes in the environment so players can learn by exploring rather than reading a manual. A real solar-particle detection archived in NASA’s DONKI database inspired the storm warning, and NASA’s lunar south-pole lighting references informed the shadow sequence. Battery blocks, event timing, and mission outcomes are simplified game rules, not NASA measurements.
